newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Maple syrup -- how sweet it is!.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Maple syrup -- how sweet it is!.

text.p: Tom and Mike Audet started tapping maple trees a full week early this year and like most New England syrup makers they expect a sweet season.

Here in the Champlain Valley, a sudden warm spell that sent temperatures well above freezing in early March caught by surprise most of the diary farmers who also make the bulk of the state's most famous crop.
"The trees were just gushing," said Tom Audet, at 45 a year older than his brother. "You have to tap when it gets warm," he said, but warm is a relative term.

Officially, sap starts running when the thermometer goes above freezing. Unofficially, "warm is when you can feel the sun on the back of your head," he said, running a big hand through the few strands of blond hair on his head.

The brothers' 120-acre (48 hectare) dairy farm, Ledge Haven, has been in the family for three generations and for three generations they have been using three stands of hard maple trees, called sugarbushes here, to make maple syrup.
"It gets in your blood," Mike said, his callused hands sticky from the last batch. "It has to. You really have to love what you're doing or else you'd be crazy to do this."

"Doing this" means going around the cold, muddy sugarbush stands, sometimes twice a day, to empty tin buckets or hoses or plastic containers that resemble IV bags filled with sap and bringing it back to the sugary, where it is boiled down over the course of several hours and made into maple syrup.
MANY TREES EQUAL LITTLE SYRUP
It takes the sap from about four maple trees to make one gallon of maple syrup.

Wearing an old lumberjacket, jeans and mud-covered boots, Mike leaned against a huge pan used in the process and explained, "It's sort of like being back in college, you know. In a good season you'll pull a couple of all-nighters hauling the sap and boiling it down. There's sort of a competition sometimes to see how long you can stay on your feet."

Sugaring season is short in New England, generally lasting only six weeks, and as the season of cold nights and warmer days wears on the color of the syrup changes from a very light copper to dark amber, accounting for the different grades of the syrup that contributes an estimated $100 million to Vermont's economy.

The season provides a much-needed economic bridge for the farmers. "It's still too early to plant and sugaring provides some extra income at a time of year when there isn't much income," Mike said as he went from the sugary to a barn where 120 Holsteins were waiting to be milked.

Sam Cutting, Sr., whose family owns Dakin Farm in Ferrisburg just north of Orwell and who has been sugaring for 37 years, explained: "Maple syrup, which does have complex flavors, differs from wine. Generally speaking, maple syrup does not age well. The whole trick to making maple syrup is making it fresh."

On the other side of the Green Mountains in the state capital, Montpelier, agriculture expert Henry Mackres, a big man with a salt-'n'-pepper beard who has been sugaring since he was a child, is proud of the product that has become his to taste and approve.
FOUR GRADES OF SYRUP, ALL SWEET

"A lot of places make maple syrup. Quebec's the No. 1 producer in the world. But nowhere is maple syrup better than Vermont," he said, explaining that fancy syrup has a lighter, more delicate flavor while dark amber has the most pronounced maple taste.

There are four grades of maple syrup depending on color and taste. "Those are really the only differences. And one isn't really better than any other. It's all a matter of personal taste," said Mackres, who prefers fancy.
John Snell, who has been sugaring for more than 20 years, said he uses the Vermont test kit and standards for maple syrup made on his farm in Buxton, Maine.

"Even though I've been doing this for a long time, I'm convinced that the more you know about maple syrup the less you really do know. You can't really tell what day it's going to run," Snell said, debunking the myth that the sap is running when the icicles are melting. Actually, sap does not run at all. It drips, much like the water from icicles.
"Sugaring is definitely a sweet way to welcome spring," Snell said.
